The action is a functional that assigns a real number to each possible configuration of the system, and it typically represents the integrated Lagrangian of the system over spacetime. In systems with fundamental units of action, its units are J·s.

virtual-work-holonomic-constraints.title: Virtual Work for Holonomic Constraints
virtual-work-holonomic-constraints.conceptual_definition: The principle of virtual work for holonomic constraints states that for a system in equilibrium, the total virtual work done by all applied forces and constraint forces during any infinitesimal virtual displacement compatible with the constraints is zero. In simpler terms, if a system is not moving (or moving at a constant velocity), the net 'effort' required to make it move infinitesimally, given the restrictions it's under, is zero.
virtual-work-holonomic-constraints.intuitive_summary: For a system in equilibrium under holonomic constraints, the total infinitesimal 'effort' or virtual work done by all forces vanishes for any physically allowed infinitesimal displacement.
virtual-work-holonomic-constraints.interpretation: The equation δW = ∑_{$k=1$}^n Q_k δq_k = 0 represents the vanishing of virtual work for a system subject to holonomic constraints. Here, δW denotes the virtual work, which is the work done by forces during a hypothetical, infinitesimal displacement (δq_k) that is consistent with the system's constraints. The term δq_k represents the generalized virtual displacement along the k-th generalized coordinate. The generalized force associated with the k-th coordinate is denoted by Q_k. These generalized forces are the effective forces that would do work if the corresponding generalized coordinate were to change. The summation ∑_{$k=1$}^n indicates that we sum over all degrees of freedom of the system, where n is the number of generalized coordinates. The equation posits that for a system in equilibrium, the total virtual work done by all forces (applied and constraint forces, when properly expressed in terms of generalized coordinates) must be zero for any virtual displacement that respects the holonomic constraints. This is a fundamental principle used to derive equations of motion or equilibrium conditions.
virtual-work-holonomic-constraints.symmetry_origin: This principle is a direct consequence of D'Alembert's principle when applied to systems in equilibrium. D'Alembert's principle extends Newton's second law to systems with constraints by considering the inertia forces. For a system in equilibrium, the net force (and thus acceleration) is zero, so the inertia forces are zero. Therefore, for equilibrium, the total virtual work done by the applied forces and the constraint forces (which are often non-conservative and can be difficult to handle directly) must be zero. For systems where the constraint forces do no virtual work (a common scenario for holonomic constraints, especially if they are workless), the principle reduces to the virtual work done by the applied forces being zero. It is also deeply connected to the concept of potential energy and the principle of minimum potential energy for conservative systems.
virtual-work-holonomic-constraints.limits_and_boundary: As the generalized forces Q_k approach zero, the virtual work also approaches zero, indicating a state of equilibrium or no applied effort. If the system has no degrees of freedom ($n=0$), the sum is empty and trivially zero, which aligns with the idea that a fixed system is in equilibrium. In the limit of infinitesimal displacements (δq_k → 0), the work done by any finite force will also be infinitesimal, consistent with the definition of virtual work. If the generalized forces are not zero but the virtual displacements compatible with constraints are zero (δq_k = 0 for all k), this implies the system is rigidly fixed, and the virtual work is zero.

\\delta W.name: Virtual Work
\\delta W.description: The infinitesimal amount of work done by forces during a virtual displacement. It is a hypothetical displacement that is infinitesimally small and compatible with the constraints of the system.

Q_k.name: Generalized Force
Q_k.description: The generalized force component corresponding to the k-th generalized coordinate. It represents the effective force that would do work if the k-th generalized coordinate were to change, taking into account all applied forces and, implicitly, constraint forces that do no virtual work.

\\delta q_k.name: Generalized Virtual Displacement
\\delta q_k.description: The infinitesimal virtual displacement along the k-th generalized coordinate. This displacement is a hypothetical change in the generalized coordinate that is consistent with the constraints of the system.

n.name: Number of Generalized Coordinates
n.description: The total number of independent generalized coordinates required to completely specify the configuration of the system. This corresponds to the number of degrees of freedom of the system.

equation-motion-mass-element.title: Equation of Motion for Mass Element
equation-motion-mass-element.conceptual_definition:
The 'Equation of Motion for Mass Element' is a fundamental expression in classical mechanics that describes how a discrete mass element responds to applied forces. It is a direct application of Newton's second law of motion, 

\[ F_{net} = ma \]

 applied to an individual component or particle within a larger system. This equation asserts that the acceleration of a mass element is directly proportional to the net force acting upon it and inversely proportional to its mass. The notation 

\[ \ddot{y}_j \]

 signifies the second time derivative of the position of the j-th mass element, which is its acceleration.
equation-motion-mass-element.intuitive_summary: The product of a mass element's mass and its acceleration is equal to the net force acting on it.
equation-motion-mass-element.interpretation:
In the equation 

\[ m \ddot{y}$_j = F_j$ \]

, the term 

\[ m \]

 represents the mass of a specific element or particle within a system. Mass is an intrinsic property of matter that quantifies its inertia, its resistance to changes in motion. The term 

\[ \ddot{y}_j \]

 denotes the second time derivative of the position 

\[ y_j \]

 of this mass element with respect to time. Physically, this is the acceleration of the j-th mass element in the y-direction (or along a specified axis). The term 

\[ F_j \]

 represents the net force acting on the j-th mass element. This net force is the vector sum of all individual forces (e.g., gravitational, electromagnetic, contact forces) acting on that mass element. The equation establishes a direct relationship: the acceleration experienced by the mass element is determined by the total force applied to it, scaled by its mass. A larger force will produce a larger acceleration, while a larger mass will result in a smaller acceleration for the same force.
equation-motion-mass-element.symmetry_origin: This equation is a direct consequence of Newton's second law of motion, which is a fundamental principle of classical mechanics. It is derived from experimental observations and forms the basis for analyzing the dynamics of systems. The equation is invariant under translations and rotations of the coordinate system, reflecting the fact that the laws of physics are the same regardless of the observer's inertial frame of reference.
equation-motion-mass-element.limits_and_boundary:
As the mass 

\[ m \rightarrow \infty \]

, for a finite force 

\[ F_j \]

, the acceleration 

\[ \ddot{y}_j \rightarrow 0 \]

. This signifies that infinitely massive objects are essentially stationary or their motion is imperceptible under finite forces. Conversely, as the mass 

\[ m \rightarrow 0 \]

 (approaching a massless particle, though strictly speaking classical mechanics does not have truly massless particles except photons which are described by quantum mechanics), for a finite force 

\[ F_j \]

, the acceleration 

\[ \ddot{y}_j \rightarrow \infty \]

. This implies that even infinitesimal forces can cause enormous accelerations for very small masses. If the net force 

\[ F_j \rightarrow 0 \]

, then for any finite mass 

\[ m \]

, the acceleration 

\[ \ddot{y}_j \rightarrow 0 \]

, which is consistent with Newton's first law (an object remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external force).

m.name: Mass
m.description: The mass of the j-th element or particle. It represents the inertia of the object, quantifying its resistance to acceleration.

y_j.name: Position of j-th mass element
y_j.description: The position coordinate of the j-th mass element in a specific direction (e.g., y-axis). This is a function of time.

\\ddot{y}_j.name: Acceleration of j-th mass element
\\ddot{y}_j.description: The second time derivative of the position of the j-th mass element, representing its acceleration in the specified direction. It is the rate of change of velocity.

F_j.name: Net Force on j-th mass element
F_j.description: The vector sum of all external forces acting on the j-th mass element. In this one-dimensional representation, it refers to the net force component along the y-axis.

energy-levels-box.title: Energy levels in a box
energy-levels-box.conceptual_definition: The formula defines the kinetic energy of a particle in terms of its momentum and mass. It is a fundamental relationship in classical mechanics, describing the energy associated with the motion of an object. This expression is derived from the definition of momentum and the relativistic energy-momentum relation in the low-velocity limit.
energy-levels-box.intuitive_summary: A heavier or faster-moving object possesses more kinetic energy.
energy-levels-box.interpretation: The equation states that the kinetic energy, denoted by $E_k$, is directly proportional to the square of the momentum, $\mathbf{p}$, and inversely proportional to twice the mass, $m$, of the particle. Momentum itself is the product of mass and velocity ($\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$), so $E_k = (m\mathbf{v})^2 / (2m) = \frac{1}{2}m\mathbf{v}^2$, which is the more familiar form of kinetic energy. This formula highlights that momentum is a more fundamental quantity from which kinetic energy can be directly computed. It is particularly useful in quantum mechanics and relativity where momentum plays a central role in describing particle states.
energy-levels-box.symmetry_origin: This formula is derived from the relativistic energy-momentum relation $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$. For a particle at rest, $E_0 = mc^2$. For a moving particle, the total energy is $E = E_0 + E_k = mc^2 + E_k$. Substituting this into the relativistic relation and expanding for small velocities (where $p \ll mc$), one can approximate $E_k = p^2$ / (2m)$. It is also a direct consequence of the definition of momentum and the work-energy theorem.
energy-levels-box.limits_and_boundary: As momentum $\mathbf{p}$ approaches zero (i.e., the particle is at rest or has negligible velocity), the kinetic energy $E_k$ also approaches zero, as $E_k \propto \mathbf{p}^2$. As mass $m$ approaches zero (for a fixed momentum), the kinetic energy approaches infinity, which reflects the difficulty of accelerating massless particles. In the limit of very high momentum (relativistic speeds), this formula becomes inaccurate, and the relativistic energy-momentum relation must be used.

E_k.name: Kinetic Energy
E_k.description: The energy of motion possessed by an object. It is measured in Joules (J).

\\mathbf{p}.name: Momentum
\\mathbf{p}.description: A vector quantity representing the mass in motion. It is defined as the product of mass and velocity (p = mv) and measured in kilogram-meters per second (kg m/s).

m.name: Mass
m.description: A fundamental property of matter that is a measure of its resistance to acceleration. In this context, it is the mass of the particle whose kinetic energy is being calculated. It is measured in kilograms (kg).

galilean-transformation-x-direction.title: Galilean transformation (x-direction)
galilean-transformation-x-direction.equation: x' = x - vt, \quad y' = y, \quad z' = z
galilean-transformation-x-direction.conceptual_definition: The Galilean transformation provides a set of equations that relate the coordinates of an event as observed in one inertial frame of reference to the coordinates of the same event as observed in another inertial frame of reference that is moving at a constant velocity relative to the first. Specifically, the provided equations describe the transformation for motion purely along the x-axis.
galilean-transformation-x-direction.intuitive_summary: The position of an event in a moving frame is its position in a stationary frame minus the distance the moving frame has traveled.
galilean-transformation-x-direction.interpretation: The Galilean transformation equations describe how the spatial coordinates of an event change between two inertial frames of reference, S and S', which are moving relative to each other. Let S be a stationary frame and S' be a frame moving with a constant velocity \(v\) in the positive x-direction relative to S. If an event occurs at coordinates \((x, y, z)\) in frame S, and the origins of S and S' coincide at time \($t=0\$), then the coordinates of the same event in frame S' are given by \((x', y', z')\). The equation \(x' = $x - vt\$) indicates that the x-coordinate in the moving frame S' is the x-coordinate in the stationary frame S minus the distance \(vt\) that the frame S' has moved along the x-axis up to time \(t\). The equations \(y' = y\) and \(z' = z\) signify that the y and z coordinates remain unchanged because the relative motion between the frames is exclusively along the x-axis. These transformations are fundamental to classical mechanics and assume that time is absolute, meaning \(t' = t\).
galilean-transformation-x-direction.symmetry_origin: The Galilean transformations originate from the principle of relativity in classical mechanics, which states that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames of reference. This implies that there is no preferred inertial frame, and hence, transformations must preserve the form of physical laws. In classical mechanics, this leads to the invariance of Newton's laws of motion under these transformations.
galilean-transformation-x-direction.limits_and_boundary: As the relative velocity \(v\) approaches zero, the Galilean transformation simplifies to \(x' = x\), \(y' = y\), \(z' = z\), indicating that the two frames are essentially the same. This corresponds to the limit where the moving frame is not moving relative to the stationary frame. Conversely, as \(v\) becomes very large, the transformation implies that space and time are no longer absolute, which hints at the breakdown of Galilean relativity at speeds approaching the speed of light, where special relativity's Lorentz transformations become necessary.

x'.name: x-coordinate in the moving frame
x'.description: The position of an event along the x-axis as measured by an observer in the moving inertial frame S'.

x.name: x-coordinate in the stationary frame
x.description: The position of an event along the x-axis as measured by an observer in the stationary inertial frame S.

v.name: Relative velocity
v.description: The constant velocity of the moving inertial frame S' relative to the stationary inertial frame S, in the positive x-direction.

t.name: Time
t.description: The time at which the event is observed. In Galilean relativity, time is absolute, meaning it is the same for all inertial observers, so $t' = t$.

y'.name: y-coordinate in the moving frame
y'.description: The position of an event along the y-axis as measured by an observer in the moving inertial frame S'.

y.name: y-coordinate in the stationary frame
y.description: The position of an event along the y-axis as measured by an observer in the stationary inertial frame S.

z'.name: z-coordinate in the moving frame
z'.description: The position of an event along the z-axis as measured by an observer in the moving inertial frame S'.

z.name: z-coordinate in the stationary frame
z.description: The position of an event along the z-axis as measured by an observer in the stationary inertial frame S.

components-four-momentum.title: Components of four-momentum
components-four-momentum.conceptual_definition: The four-momentum, denoted by the contravariant four-vector $P^\mu$, is a fundamental concept in special relativity that unifies the classical concepts of energy and linear momentum into a single entity. It is a relativistic generalization of momentum, incorporating energy as its time component and three-momentum as its spatial components. This unification arises from the structure of spacetime as described by Minkowski geometry.
components-four-momentum.intuitive_summary: Four-momentum combines an object's energy and momentum into a single relativistic quantity that transforms consistently under Lorentz transformations.
components-four-momentum.interpretation: The four-momentum $P^\mu$ is expressed as a four-vector with components $(P^0, P^1, P^2, P^3)$. In the first form, $P^\mu = (E/c, \mathbf{p})$, the components are given by the energy $E$ divided by the speed of light $c$ as the time-like component ($P^0$), and the three-dimensional momentum vector $\mathbf{p}$ as the space-like components ($P^1, P^2, P^3$). This form highlights the relationship between energy and momentum. In the second form, $P^\mu = (\gamma m c, \gamma m \mathbf{v})$, the components are expressed in terms of the rest mass $m$ of the particle, the Lorentz factor $\gamma$, the speed of light $c$, and the particle's three-velocity $\mathbf{v}$. The time-like component is $P^0 = \gamma$ m c$, which is the relativistic energy $E$ divided by $c$ (since $E = \gamma$ m c^2$). The space-like components are $P^i = \gamma$ m v^i$, which constitute the relativistic momentum $\mathbf{p} = \gamma m \mathbf{v}$. The Lorentz factor $\$gamma = 1 / \sqrt${$1 - v^2/c^2$}$ accounts for relativistic effects as the velocity $v$ approaches the speed of light.
components-four-momentum.symmetry_origin: The four-momentum arises from the principle of conservation of energy and momentum in a relativistic framework. In Minkowski spacetime, physical laws are covariant under Lorentz transformations. Quantities that are conserved in all inertial frames are often represented as four-vectors. The four-momentum is the generator of spacetime translations, meaning its conservation is directly linked to the homogeneity of spacetime. Its definition ensures that the relativistic energy-momentum relation ($E^2 - (pc)^2 = (mc^2)^2$) is Lorentz invariant.
components-four-momentum.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of low velocities, where $v 	o 0$, the Lorentz factor $\gamma 	o 1$. In this non-relativistic limit, the four-momentum simplifies: $P^0 = mc$ (a constant term related to rest mass energy, often ignored in non-relativistic energy calculations where only kinetic energy is considered) and $\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$. This recovers the classical definition of momentum. As the velocity $v$ approaches the speed of light $c$, $v 	o c$, the Lorentz factor $\gamma 	o \infty$. Consequently, both the energy $E = \gamma$ mc^2$ and the magnitude of the momentum $\mathbf{p} = \gamma m \mathbf{v}$ approach infinity, indicating that a massive particle cannot reach the speed of light.

P^\\mu.name: Four-momentum
P^\\mu.description: The relativistic four-vector representing the combination of energy and momentum of a particle or system. The superscript \(\mu\) indicates it is a contravariant vector in spacetime, typically taking values 0, 1, 2, 3.

E.name: Relativistic Energy
E.description: The total energy of a particle, including its rest mass energy and kinetic energy, in an inertial frame. In special relativity, it is given by \(E = \gamma m c^2\).

c.name: Speed of Light in Vacuum
c.description: The universal constant representing the speed of light in a vacuum, approximately \(299,792,458\) m/s.

\\mathbf{p}.name: Three-momentum
\\mathbf{p}.description: The relativistic three-dimensional momentum vector of a particle. In special relativity, it is given by \(\mathbf{p} = \gamma m \mathbf{v}\).

m.name: Rest Mass
m.description: The invariant mass of a particle, measured in its rest frame. It is a fundamental property of the particle.

\\gamma.name: Lorentz Factor
\\gamma.description: The relativistic factor \(\gamma = 1 / \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}\), which quantifies the degree to which relativistic effects are significant. It depends on the particle's speed \(v\).

\\mathbf{v}.name: Three-velocity
\\mathbf{v}.description: The three-dimensional velocity vector of a particle in a given inertial frame.

divergence-theorem.title: Divergence theorem
divergence-theorem.conceptual_definition: The Divergence Theorem, also known as Gauss's Theorem or Ostrogradsky's Theorem, is a fundamental result in vector calculus that relates a volume integral of the divergence of a vector field to a surface integral of the flux of that same vector field across the boundary of the volume. It essentially states that the total outward flux of a vector field through a closed surface is equal to the volume integral of the divergence of that field within the enclosed volume.
divergence-theorem.intuitive_summary: The total outward flow of a vector field from a closed region is equal to the net 'source strength' within that region.
divergence-theorem.interpretation: The left side of the equation, ∫_V ∇ · ̅F dV, represents the total divergence of the vector field ̅F integrated over a volume V. The divergence, ∇ · ̅F, is a scalar quantity that measures the extent to which a vector field flows outward from a point (a positive divergence indicates a source, a negative divergence indicates a sink, and zero divergence indicates a source-free field). Therefore, the volume integral quantifies the net 'source strength' or net outward flow from all points within the volume. The right side of the equation, ∫_{∂} ̅F · da, represents the flux of the vector field ̅F across the closed boundary surface ∂V. The dot product ̅F · da calculates the component of the vector field perpendicular to the infinitesimal surface element da, and the integral sums this outward flux over the entire boundary. The Divergence Theorem establishes that these two quantities are always equal: the total outward flux of a vector field across a closed surface is precisely equal to the integral of the divergence of that field throughout the enclosed volume. This theorem is crucial in many areas of physics, including electromagnetism (Gauss's law for electric fields), fluid dynamics, and gravitation.
divergence-theorem.symmetry_origin: The Divergence Theorem can be derived from the fundamental properties of vector calculus and integration. It can be proven by considering the integral of the divergence of a vector field in Cartesian coordinates and then performing integration by parts, which leads to surface integrals. Conceptually, it stems from the idea of local conservation laws. If a quantity is conserved within a region, then any net change in that quantity must be accounted for by the flux across its boundary. The theorem is invariant under coordinate transformations, reflecting the underlying physical principles it describes.
divergence-theorem.limits_and_boundary: In the limit as the volume V approaches a point, the Divergence Theorem becomes the definition of the divergence at that point. If the vector field ̅F is identically zero everywhere within the volume, then both sides of the equation are zero, which is consistent. If the vector field has zero divergence everywhere within the volume (∇ · ̅$F = 0$), then the net flux through any closed surface enclosing any part of that volume is zero. The theorem applies to any sufficiently smooth vector field and any piecewise smooth, closed surface.

\\int_V.name: Volume Integral
\\int_V.description: The integral of a quantity over a three-dimensional volume V.

\\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf{F}.name: Divergence of Vector Field
\\nabla \\cdot \\mathbf{F}.description: The divergence of the vector field \mathbf{F}. It measures the rate at which the vector field flows outward from a point. For a velocity field \mathbf{v}, its unit is s^{-1}.

dV.name: Volume Element
dV.description: An infinitesimal element of volume within the region V.

\\oint_{\\partial V}.name: Surface Integral
\\oint_{\\partial V}.description: The integral of a quantity over a closed surface \partial V, which is the boundary of the volume V.

\\mathbf{F}.name: Vector Field
\\mathbf{F}.description: A vector field defined over the volume V. The units depend on the physical context, e.g., for force per area it would be N/m^2.

d\\mathbf{a}.name: Area Element Vector
d\\mathbf{a}.description: An infinitesimal vector representing a surface element on the boundary \partial V. Its magnitude is the area of the element, and its direction is normal to the surface, pointing outward.

curie-law-paramagnetism.title: Curie's Law for paramagnetism
curie-law-paramagnetism.conceptual_definition: Curie's Law describes the magnetic susceptibility of a paramagnetic material at a given temperature and in the presence of a magnetic field. It quantifies the magnetization (M) induced in the material, stating that it is directly proportional to the applied magnetic field strength (B) and inversely proportional to the absolute temperature (T). This relationship arises from the thermal agitation of atomic magnetic moments, which tend to align with an external magnetic field, but are opposed by random thermal motion.
curie-law-paramagnetism.intuitive_summary: The stronger the external magnetic field, the more ordered the magnetic moments become, increasing magnetization, while higher temperatures provide more thermal energy to randomize these moments, thus reducing magnetization.
curie-law-paramagnetism.interpretation: The equation, \( $M = C$ \frac{B}{T} \), relates the macroscopic magnetization \( M \) of a paramagnetic material to the applied magnetic field \( B \) and the absolute temperature \( T \). The variable \( M \) represents the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume of the material, typically measured in Amperes per meter (A/m). The variable \( B \) is the magnetic flux density, also known as the magnetic field strength, measured in Teslas (T). The absolute temperature \( T \) is measured in Kelvin (K). The constant \( C \) is known as the Curie constant, which is a material-specific property that depends on the number density of magnetic moments and their individual magnetic moments. A higher Curie constant indicates a greater response to the magnetic field.
curie-law-paramagnetism.symmetry_origin: Curie's Law originates from statistical mechanics, specifically from the Langevin or Brillouin treatments of paramagnetic behavior. It arises from considering the thermal equilibrium between the orienting effect of an external magnetic field on individual magnetic dipoles and the randomizing effect of thermal energy. The derivation involves averaging over the orientations of magnetic dipoles in a thermal bath, considering the Boltzmann distribution of energies.
curie-law-paramagnetism.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of very low temperatures or very strong magnetic fields (where \( B/T \) becomes large), Curie's Law breaks down. This is because the magnetic moments become almost completely aligned with the field, and the magnetization approaches its saturation value, which is limited by the total number of magnetic moments in the material. In the limit of very high temperatures or very weak magnetic fields (where \( B/T \) approaches zero), the magnetization becomes very small, tending towards zero, as the thermal agitation dominates the ordering effect of the field.

M.name: Magnetization
M.description: The magnetic dipole moment per unit volume of the paramagnetic material. It represents the net magnetic strength of the material induced by an external field.

C.name: Curie Constant
C.description: A material-specific constant that quantifies the strength of paramagnetism. It depends on the density of magnetic moments and the magnitude of individual atomic magnetic moments.

B.name: Magnetic Flux Density
B.description: The strength of the external magnetic field applied to the material, also known as magnetic field strength.

T.name: Absolute Temperature
T.description: The thermodynamic temperature of the paramagnetic material, measured on the Kelvin scale.
